questions.q: How many hydrogen atoms are there in 4.25 g of ammonia, \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\)? (\(M_{\text{r}} = 17.0\); \(L = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: Amount of ammonia: \(\frac{4.25}{17.0} = 0.250\ \text{mol}\). Each molecule has three hydrogen atoms, so hydrogen atoms = \(0.250 \times 3 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23}\) = \(4.52 \times 10^{23}\). (Stopping at the number of molecules leads to \(1.51 \times 10^{23}\).)

questions.q: What amount of sodium hydroxide is in \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of a \(0.200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) solution?
questions.solution: Convert the volume to \(\text{dm}^{3}\): \(\frac{25.0}{1000} = 0.0250\ \text{dm}^{3}\). Amount = concentration × volume = \(0.200 \times 0.0250\) = \(5.00 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}\). (Leaving the volume in \(\text{cm}^{3}\) leads to 5.00 mol.)

questions.q: What amount of gas occupies \(500\ \text{cm}^{3}\) at \(100\ \text{kPa}\) and \(27\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\)? (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: Use SI units: \(p = 1.00 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}\), \(V = 5.00 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{3}\), \(T = 300\ \text{K}\). Then \(n = \frac{pV}{RT} = \frac{1.00 \times 10^{5} \times 5.00 \times 10^{-4}}{8.31 \times 300}\) = 0.0201 mol. (Using the temperature in degrees Celsius leads to 0.223 mol.)

questions.q: A 0.250 g sample of a volatile liquid is vaporised. The vapour occupies \(98.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) at \(101\ \text{kPa}\) and \(373\ \text{K}\). What is the relative molecular mass of the liquid? (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: \(n = \frac{pV}{RT} = \frac{1.01 \times 10^{5} \times 9.80 \times 10^{-5}}{8.31 \times 373} = 3.19 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}\). Then \(M_{\text{r}} = \frac{0.250}{3.19 \times 10^{-3}}\) = 78.3. (Leaving the pressure in kPa leads to \(7.83 \times 10^{4}\).)

questions.q: A compound contains 24.3% carbon, 4.1% hydrogen and 71.6% chlorine by mass. Its relative molecular mass is 99.0. What is its molecular formula? (\(A_{\text{r}}\): C = 12.0, H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5)
questions.solution: Divide by \(A_{\text{r}}\): C \(\frac{24.3}{12.0} = 2.03\), H \(\frac{4.1}{1.0} = 4.1\), Cl \(\frac{71.6}{35.5} = 2.02\). The ratio is 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is \(\mathrm{CH_{2}Cl}\), mass 49.5. Since \(\frac{99.0}{49.5} = 2\), the molecular formula is \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}Cl_{2}}\). (Stopping at the empirical formula is the usual slip.)

questions.q: A 2.46 g sample of hydrated magnesium sulfate, \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4} \cdot \mathit{x}H_{2}O}\), is heated to constant mass. The anhydrous solid left has a mass of 1.20 g. What is the value of \(x\)? (\(M_{\text{r}}\): \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}}\) = 120.4, \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) = 18.0)
questions.solution: Mass of water lost = 2.46 − 1.20 = 1.26 g. Amounts: \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}}\) \(\frac{1.20}{120.4} = 0.00997\ \text{mol}\); water \(\frac{1.26}{18.0} = 0.0700\ \text{mol}\). Ratio \(\frac{0.0700}{0.00997} = 7.02\), so \(x\) = 7. (Comparing the masses instead of the amounts leads to 1.)

questions.q: Iron is extracted by the reaction \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3} + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_{2}}\). What is the maximum mass of iron that can be made from 80.0 g of iron(III) oxide? (\(M_{\text{r}}\) \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}\) = 159.6; \(A_{\text{r}}\) Fe = 55.8)
questions.solution: Amount of \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}\) = \(\frac{80.0}{159.6} = 0.501\ \text{mol}\). Each mole gives 2 mol of Fe, so 1.00 mol of Fe, and mass = \(1.00 \times 55.8\) = 55.9 g. (Missing the 1 : 2 ratio leads to 28.0 g.)

questions.q: Butane burns completely: \(\mathrm{2C_{4}H_{10}(g) + 13O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 8CO_{2}(g) + 10H_{2}O(l)}\). What volume of oxygen is needed to burn \(40\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of butane, both volumes measured at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.solution: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal amounts, so volumes react in the ratio of the equation, 2 : 13. Oxygen needed = \(40 \times \frac{13}{2}\) = \(260\ \text{cm}^{3}\). (Multiplying by 13 without dividing by 2 leads to \(520\ \text{cm}^{3}\).)

questions.q: Sodium hydrogencarbonate decomposes on heating: \(\mathrm{2NaHCO_{3}(s) \rightarrow Na_{2}CO_{3}(s) + CO_{2}(g) + H_{2}O(g)}\). What mass of \(\mathrm{NaHCO_{3}}\) must be heated to give \(360\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of carbon dioxide at room temperature and pressure? (\(M_{\text{r}}\) \(\mathrm{NaHCO_{3}}\) = 84.0; molar volume of a gas = \(24.0\ \text{dm}^{3}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: Amount of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) = \(\frac{0.360}{24.0} = 0.0150\ \text{mol}\). The equation needs 2 mol of \(\mathrm{NaHCO_{3}}\) per mole of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), so 0.0300 mol, and mass = \(0.0300 \times 84.0\) = 2.52 g. (Using a 1 : 1 ratio leads to 1.26 g; leaving the volume in \(\text{cm}^{3}\) leads to 2520 g.)

questions.q: A \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) portion of sodium carbonate solution needs \(22.50\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) hydrochloric acid for complete reaction: \(\mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3} + 2HCl \rightarrow 2NaCl + H_{2}O + CO_{2}}\). What is the concentration of the sodium carbonate solution?
questions.solution: Amount of HCl = \(0.100 \times 0.02250 = 2.25 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}\). Sodium carbonate reacts 1 : 2, so it is \(1.125 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}\) in \(0.0250\ \text{dm}^{3}\). Concentration = \(\frac{1.125 \times 10^{-3}}{0.0250}\) = \(0.0450\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\). (Ignoring the 1 : 2 ratio leads to \(0.0900\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\).)

questions.q: A 0.500 g sample of impure calcium carbonate is added to \(50.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) hydrochloric acid, an excess. The acid left over needs \(22.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) sodium hydroxide. What is the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in the sample? (\(\mathrm{CaCO_{3} + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_{2} + H_{2}O + CO_{2}}\); \(M_{\text{r}}\) \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) = 100.1)
questions.solution: HCl added = \(0.200 \times 0.0500 = 0.0100\ \text{mol}\). HCl left over = NaOH used = \(0.100 \times 0.0220 = 0.00220\ \text{mol}\). HCl that reacted = 0.00780 mol, so \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) = 0.00390 mol = \(0.00390 \times 100.1 = 0.390\ \text{g}\). Percentage = \(\frac{0.390}{0.500} \times 100\) = 78.1%. (Working from the leftover acid as if it had reacted leads to 22.0%.)

questions.q: Burning 12.0 g of magnesium in air gives 16.0 g of magnesium oxide: \(\mathrm{2Mg + O_{2} \rightarrow 2MgO}\). What is the percentage yield? (\(A_{\text{r}}\) Mg = 24.3; \(M_{\text{r}}\) MgO = 40.3)
questions.solution: Amount of Mg = \(\frac{12.0}{24.3} = 0.494\ \text{mol}\), which gives at most 0.494 mol of MgO = \(0.494 \times 40.3 = 19.9\ \text{g}\). Percentage yield = \(\frac{16.0}{19.9} \times 100\) = 80.4%. (Comparing the two masses directly, \(\frac{12.0}{16.0}\), leads to 75.0%.)

questions.q: Ethanol can be made by fermentation: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} \rightarrow 2C_{2}H_{5}OH + 2CO_{2}}\). What is the percentage atom economy for making ethanol? (\(M_{\text{r}}\): \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}}\) = 180.0, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH}\) = 46.0, \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) = 44.0)
questions.solution: Atom economy = \(\frac{\text{mass of desired product}}{\text{total mass of reactants}} \times 100\). Two moles of ethanol form: \(\frac{2 \times 46.0}{180.0} \times 100\) = 51.1%. (Forgetting the 2 in front of ethanol leads to 25.6%; the carbon dioxide accounts for the other 48.9%.)

questions.q: Aqueous silver nitrate is added to aqueous sodium chloride and a white precipitate forms. Which is the ionic equation for the reaction?
questions.solution: An ionic equation shows only the ions that change; sodium and nitrate ions are spectator ions and stay in solution. The precipitate is solid silver chloride: \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq) + Cl^{-}(aq) \rightarrow AgCl(s)}\). (The full equation is correct but is not the ionic equation; the precipitate must have the state symbol (s).)

questions.q: Which is the correctly balanced equation for the reaction of aluminium with sulfuric acid?
questions.solution: Aluminium forms \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) and sulfate is \(\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}\), so the salt is \(\mathrm{Al_{2}(SO_{4})_{3}}\). Three \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\) supply six hydrogen atoms, which form three \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) molecules: \(\mathrm{2Al + 3H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow Al_{2}(SO_{4})_{3} + 3H_{2}}\). (Hydrogen gas is diatomic, so it is never written as H.)

questions.q: A burette can be read to \(\pm 0.05\ \text{cm}^{3}\). A titre is found from an initial reading of \(0.50\ \text{cm}^{3}\) and a final reading of \(24.60\ \text{cm}^{3}\). What is the percentage uncertainty in the titre?
questions.solution: The titre is 24.60 − 0.50 = \(24.10\ \text{cm}^{3}\). It comes from two readings, each \(\pm 0.05\ \text{cm}^{3}\), so the uncertainty is \(\pm 0.10\ \text{cm}^{3}\). Percentage uncertainty = \(\frac{0.10}{24.10} \times 100\) = 0.41%. (Counting only one reading leads to 0.21%.)

questions.q: A student's titres are about \(12\ \text{cm}^{3}\). Which change to the method would reduce the percentage uncertainty in each titre?

options.A: Use a burette that can only be read to the nearest \(0.1\ \text{cm}^{3}\).
options.B: Use a smaller volume of the solution in the conical flask.
options.C: Use a more concentrated solution in the burette.
options.D: Use a more dilute solution in the burette, so that each titre is larger.

questions.solution: The burette's uncertainty is fixed, about \(\pm 0.10\ \text{cm}^{3}\) per titre, so a larger titre makes it a smaller percentage. A more dilute solution in the burette (or a larger volume in the flask) gives a larger titre. (Making the titrant more concentrated, or using less solution in the flask, makes the titre smaller and the percentage uncertainty larger.)

questions.q: For which substance should the term relative formula mass be used rather than relative molecular mass?
questions.solution: Relative molecular mass applies to substances made of molecules. Sodium chloride is ionic, a giant lattice with no molecules, so its formula unit has a relative formula mass. The other three are simple molecular substances. (A large formula does not make a substance ionic: glucose is molecular.)

questions.q: Which sample contains the greatest number of atoms? (\(A_{\text{r}}\): H = 1.0, He = 4.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0)
questions.solution: Find the amount of atoms in each. Hydrogen: 1.0 mol of \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\), 2.0 mol of atoms. Helium: 1.0 mol of atoms. Oxygen: 1.0 mol of \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\), 2.0 mol of atoms. Methane: \(\frac{8.0}{16.0} = 0.50\ \text{mol}\) of molecules, each of five atoms, so 2.5 mol of atoms. The answer is the 8.0 g of methane. (Comparing amounts of molecules rather than atoms makes the samples look equal.)

questions.q: \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(2.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) hydrochloric acid is diluted to exactly \(250\ \text{cm}^{3}\) with water in a volumetric flask. What amount of HCl is in a \(10.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) portion of the diluted solution?
questions.solution: Diluting tenfold, from \(25.0\) to \(250\ \text{cm}^{3}\), gives \(0.200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\). Amount in \(10.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) = \(0.200 \times 0.0100\) = \(2.00 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}\). (Forgetting the dilution leads to \(2.00 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol}\).)
